{"self_assessment": "Impact: I laid the lower tail piece, which stayed live to the tip and never needed rework. I then built the back half of the bottom body line from the crossing forward and laid the join to meet Maya's line in the middle, so the bottom line connected through. Late on, I cleared the upper tail jams and lifted stray pale dominoes past the tail so Maya had enough to finish the notch. When time was called the run was reaching most of the standing dominoes, but I can't say the fork's inner notch was fully closed. That was the last open item and it was Maya's.

Execution: I checked the crossing and the tail by eye and gave the table accurate reads. For example, I told Priya the lower tail was already live and the pale bits below the crossing were just an unconnected stray, which saved a needless re-join. I made one mistake: I clipped my own join and knocked down a few dominoes near my end, and had to stand them back up, which delayed the bottom join. I also said I'd look over the tail tip, but Tom's relay and Maya's notch work meant I added little there beyond the jam fixes.

Collaboration: I stayed off pieces other people owned (Tom's upper tail, Maya's notch) to avoid bumps, and I said so out loud. I also kept asking where people had stopped so I could join up. When the dominoes ran low, I freed stock for Maya.

Leadership: I didn't lead the plan. Priya set the design and assignments, and I followed them. What I did contribute was clear status calls, such as naming the notch as the last open spot, and steering effort there rather than redoing parts that already worked. With more time I would have been quicker to flag the notch risk and offer to take the lower open end myself."}
